stories.title_en: Matrix Multiplication is Θ(n^2.25) [pdf]

comments.author: zone411
comments.text:
For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked,
https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/
).
They include:
#25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture.
#89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for
#64 — Mean-payoff games,
#65 — Parity games,
#340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games.
#183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes,
#130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart.
#137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound.
(rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).

comments.author: mmaunder
comments.text:
One possibility is that OpenAI may be holding back their best models to make fundamental breakthroughs, then using those breakthroughs to build stronger models in a compounding loop. If they were playing this game, public model quality would stall as compute shifted to internal research, and occasional releases like this would provide a glimpse of  more beneath the surface.
Edit: Forgot to point out that this came from an unreleased model and the recipe isn't disclosed. And they've been doing this kind of thing since August.

If even the prestige from Riemann's Hypothesis couldn't boost ANT, what is the reason for them devoting such a huge fraction of their R&D budget to unrelated (though impactful) problems? Open weight models are to the point that most business cases are completely solved by them, at a fraction of the price of Claude, Copilot, or OpenAI. comments.author: seizethecheese
comments.text:
These math proofs are so insanely over my head, but I really want to understand them. I tried Jane Street's socratic tutor skill (
https://github.com/janestreet/agent_skills/blob/master/socra...
) against this pdf and here's what I got:
- Matrix multiplication is multiplying pairs of numbers together then summing them (you probably know this already)
- Without any optimization, this process is o(n^3)
- You can make this faster if you share a multiplication or sum across multiple places
- By sharing sums / multiplication operations the maximum efficiency is o(n^2.25)
I studied Economics, not CS so I'm a bit hazy on what big o actually means, to be honest.

stories.title_en: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed

comments.author: devy
comments.text: Frontier models today can easily figure this out. The less frontier models as of right now are probably going to take a long horizon session to figure out this type of "side channel" comms. However, posting this in depth step by step on the internet and discussed in open forums like here, now all models definitely know about this trick now.

comments.author: amluto
comments.text:
This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache.
As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question).
More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is
software
communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.

comments.author: kgeist
comments.text:
If a single vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode without disaggregation, I can think of another way.
Alice reads a long document every N seconds to transmit a 1, and does nothing to transmit a 0. Bob, in its own loop, measures the time using bash, generates some random text and writes it to a file, and then checks the time again to estimate its own tokens per second (file length / elapsed time).
The trick is that when a vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode, decoding slows down measurably because vLLM has to alternate between prefill and decode phases.
It assumes only 2 agents are running, though, but it doesn't require fine-tuning or a second helper model.

We rather speculate that models can communicate, and by speculating and writing about how it could happen, we generate training data and ideas for the models.  These models are coming along based on the rubbish we keep thinking of and documenting.

stories.title_en: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

comments.author: gopalv
comments.text:
> We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.
The ability to write code is basically the superpower for these models.
As long as what you need to do to make progress is write better code, they will do better at the task.
The last 30 years has been making more and more things run using code instead of any other mechanism (music, illustration, vfx).
Even math, the models were worse off before Lean was accepted as output.

comments.author: fabian2k
comments.text:
> To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.
I don't get it. What did GTP-6.2 actually design here? The sequence is the structure for proteins. So did the model output a sequence here as answer to a question like "design a protein for target X" or not?
To me, "protein design" means you have a goal and you create a sequence that achieves that goal. I'm also not sure what a "three-dimensional design" would be in this case. Charges matter a lot for binding, as do hydrophobic areas. At sufficient resolution you're again at an amino acid sequence in a specific fold with that. Or did GPT-6.2 just design a rough tertiary structure here (helices, beta sheets and loops) and the details were filled in by the specialized model?

comments.author: plaidfuji
comments.text:
This is interesting, although the “beyond specialized models” feels a bit premature. It seems like GPT can act like a glue layer between the highly specialized models that carry out each specific sub-task in a protein design workflow… and in some cases, can outperform specialized models at those tasks.
I’ve noticed that LLMs are very good at this type of glue work between highly specialized fields. It used to be quite difficult to “connect” your own work to adjacent tools made by other SMEs, sometimes so difficult that it was impractical.
I suspect one of the biggest impacts of LLMs on science will be the enablement of more frictionless collaboration and higher-level integration of specialized capabilities in a single study.
That said, the use of “intrinsic design capabilities” in the title of this article is misleading, as much of the demonstrated capabilities involve tool calls, and/or need outside support by the same specialized models they claim to have moved beyond in order to arrive at useful results.

Makes total sense that they'd be working on this, it's something we discussed in the lab as well as the likely future of this work - true integration of the language modeling capabilities with proteins, natively multimodal like it's done with images. Five years ago we laughed at people with galaxy brained ideas to train / fuse a protein and natural language model, advertising this idea of "give me a natural language request and the model spits out the sequence that does the thing". There are many objections - the annotated data is not there, trying to pose everything as a language modeling objective sounded really naive at the time, and there are lots of tasks that are structural/chemical in nature that require inference based on physical and chemical principles, which interpolating machine learning models shouldn't be able to do. Most of these objections still exist, but now we aren't laughing. I do think eventually these models will get there.

comments.author: Xcelerate
comments.text:
I heard an interesting question once: if we consider all the greatest discoveries of mankind and imagine a counterfactual world where their discoverer had not existed, how many additional years would it have taken for someone else to have made the discovery?
Subjectively, I think most of the major discoveries would have only been delayed by a decade or two. E.g., general relativity, quantum mechanics, the laws of thermodynamics.
For the incompleteness theorems, however, I’m not sure that we would even be aware of them today without Gödel. Tarski might have come the closest, but there were still a few insane conceptual leaps that had to be made beyond the undefinability of truth.
The theorems are often considered a curiosity at the edges of mathematics, but I’m not so sure. I think they might be more fundamental than typically given credit for. The problem is that the theorems aren’t really actionable since they rule out essentially all algorithmic methods of working around the limitations they entail.

stories.title_en: An Italian folding bicycle design that fits into a suitcase

comments.author: asdff
comments.text: It takes some learning curve, but a skateboard is actually a really good way to get around an urban area. Biggest pluses are you can tuck it away anywhere, but unlike a folding bike, you can use it instantly. You end up saving time in all sorts of places that would be inappropriate with other vehicles, thanks to the speed differential being closer to a couple mile an hour walking than most other micro mobility that's closer to a 25mph car. Biking down the mezzanine to the train platform is a little egregious, but pushing a skateboard out of anyone's way is perfectly reasonable, and might save you quite a lot of time to make that train connection. Any clear patch of 25 feet in front of you, you might as well skate it in a half second.

stories.title_en: GTA 6 Running on Windows

comments.author: ivraatiems
comments.text:
I just don't see this as deadly to the production of games the way others do. GTA 6 is a monumental human achievement in video games - in fact it's arguably one of the largest artistic endeavors ever undertaken. If numbers are to believed, it has also already made around $4 billion against a $1-2 billion budget. It is massively profitable, and doubtless will become more so as DLC and a real PC port are released.
I see this, instead, as a continuation of the usual pushback against the lockdown of entertainment to certain media. I personally haven't bought the game yet because I don't have or intend to buy an Xbox! It's deeply frustrating that everyone else will get to experience it before me because I didn't want to spend hundreds of dollars on a console!
But I will probably still buy it when it comes out on PC, even if this port works.

comments.author: Tiberium
comments.text:
For the general picture: the Xbox version of the game was leaked by Cyberleek - first the resources, then the game binary.
Because modern Xbox is very close to a Windows PC with some extra Xbox stuff, running the actual game code isn't hard, it's mostly about compatibility and graphics, plus the binary doesn't have any special DRM/obfuscation.
The current projects (xcl and VIctory) basically take a Wine-like approach. The main problems they have to solve, as I understand:
- The game ships with raw RDNA 2 shaders, so the projects have to translate that to another format, e.g. DXIL for DirectX 12, and compile those shaders. So you need a good translation/recompilation pipeline, if it's bad, the shaders will be bloated and perform poorly
- Xbox has unified memory, while most PCs do not, so you have to add a lot of workarounds and book-keeping for the game to work properly with that
- Xbox's DirectX 12 differs from the normal Windows one in some ways, and the game uses Xbox-specific texture formats with DirectStorage
